candidate_paragraph_changes.old: Page screening in sparse attention can discard useful distant tokens before refinement, making its scoring representation a critical part of candidate selection. We study a near--far cascade whose page screening and token refinement share 32 low-frequency RoPE coordinates, arranged as 16 complete rotation pairs. Separate regional page quotas retain candidate access to near and far history, while final attention uses the selected original-dimensional keys and values. In an archived configuration with 128-token prefix and recent protection, on five LongBench tasks with Qwen3-8B, the shared-subspace configuration uses 32 active coordinates for both page and token scoring and averages 47.588. Nominal variants with full-dimensional page scoring (128/32 active coordinates) or token scoring (32/128) score 47.910 and 47.666, respectively. The available records do not establish matched configurations, so these score differences are descriptive. A separate synthetic study reports no selector-latency reduction for the shared-subspace configuration relative to the nominal page-scoring variant. The results motivate evaluating compact scoring jointly with selection quality and preparation-inclusive cost, without establishing a joint quality--latency advantage.
candidate_paragraph_changes.new: Sparse attention must decide which history remains accessible before evaluating attention on a bounded token set. We study the trade-off between candidate access and selection cost at a fixed final token budget. Our near--far cascade combines two mechanisms: a shared 32-coordinate RoPE scoring map for page screening and token refinement, and separate regional page quotas. Final attention uses original-dimensional queries, keys and values. On five Qwen3-8B LongBench tasks, an archived 128/128-protection configuration scores 47.588, compared with 47.910 and 47.666 for nominal full-dimensional page- and token-scoring variants. These descriptive comparisons do not isolate scoring dimensionality or validate the current compact 4/128-protection candidate. Separate synthetic timings show no selector-latency reduction, and historical model-level measurements remain slower than dense attention. We therefore present a design and preliminary evaluation, not an established quality--latency improvement. candidate_paragraph_changes.old:
Long-context sparse attention must retain useful history while making selection cheaper than the attention it removes. In a two-level selector, page screening determines which tokens reach refinement; the next stage cannot recover a rejected page. Scoring dimensionality controls arithmetic per comparison, while preparation, ranking and memory access also contribute to latency. We study scoring representation and candidate allocation as distinct design choices.

We study three connected choices: shared scoring coordinates, regional candidate quotas, and an optional prefill-informed far gate (Fig.~\ref{fig:architecture}). The default near--far cascade uses the first two; the gate is a separate extension. Each layer and KV head uses one set of complete RoPE coordinate pairs for page screening and token refinement. The cascade assigns separate page quotas to recent unprotected history and the remaining history, allowing distant candidates to enter refinement even when the near region dominates page selection. Original-dimensional Q/K/V determine attention over the resulting token set. Sharing the scoring view reduces representational duplication in the design; regional quotas control candidate access. Neither mechanism alone guarantees lower latency or unchanged task quality.

Regional attention demand motivates examining candidate allocation separately from scoring representation. We therefore ask how regional page quotas change retrieval at a fixed final token budget, whether shared compact coordinates retain useful candidates, and whether attention savings exceed preparation and selection costs. Archived coordinate diagnostics motivate this separation but do not isolate frequency from coordinate-pair structure or evaluate the actual regional scoring functions. Layerwise prefill profiles likewise motivate testing the optional gate as an approximation policy, without assuming that prefill statistics bound far-region demand during decoding (Supplementary Note~S6). Motivated by ClusterKV's token/page view~\cite{clusterkv}, Figure~\ref{fig:pending-observation} shows archived dense-reference distance density and a feasible whole-bin capture diagnostic for Qwen3-8B. Regional capture differs in these observations; this does not establish selector fidelity or task quality. The available scores and local timings neither isolate stage effects nor establish a joint quality--latency advantage.
candidate_paragraph_changes.new:
Long-context sparse attention replaces full-history attention with attention over selected tokens. Selection itself, however, requires scoring, ranking and memory access. The central design question is therefore how to preserve access to useful history at a fixed final token budget without spending the saved attention cost on retrieval. A page-to-token cascade makes this tension explicit: page screening reduces the candidate support for refinement, but a useful token cannot be recovered once its page is excluded.

We examine two coupled decisions within this cascade. The scoring representation determines the information available to rank pages and tokens; regional allocation determines which parts of history can reach refinement. Reducing scoring width does not ensure that distant candidates survive page screening, while reserving distant pages does not ensure inexpensive selection. Our design combines a common low-frequency RoPE coordinate map across both stages with separate near--far page quotas. It retains original-dimensional Q/K/V for attention over the final selected set. The shared map and the regional quotas are the two core mechanisms; a prefill-informed far gate is an optional extension, disabled by default.

Figure~\ref{fig:pending-observation} motivates treating regional access separately from scoring width. Following ClusterKV's token/page perspective~\cite{clusterkv}, it contrasts distance-dependent attention density with near/far retention under one feasible global whole-bin selection. The regional retention differs across these Qwen3-8B observations, motivating a test of reserved regional capacity. This diagnostic neither evaluates our production selector nor proves that regional quotas improve task quality. Likewise, slower phase variation motivates the low-frequency coordinate choice, but its retrieval value depends on content and must be tested rather than assumed.

This work specifies a shared-map regional cascade and examines three questions: (Q1) what do the available task scores show about compact scoring, (Q2) what evidence supports regional candidate access, and (Q3) do the reported costs justify the reduction in attention support? The evaluation separates historical configuration scores, regional diagnostics and timing measurements rather than combining them into a matched quality--latency result. It reports no established joint advantage: the current compact 4/128-protection candidate lacks matched validation, local selector time does not decrease, and historical sparse decoding remains slower than dense attention. These limits define the status of the design as a research candidate.

本文研究三项相互关联的选择：共享评分坐标、区域候选配额，以及可选的预填充远区门控（图\ref{fig:architecture}）。默认近远级联采用前两项，门控作为单独扩展。每层、每KV头的页筛选和词元精筛采用同一组完整RoPE坐标对。级联为近期未保护历史与其余历史分别分配页配额，使远端词元即使在近区主导页选择时仍能进入精筛。最终注意力在所选词元集合上使用原始全维查询、键和值。共享评分视图减少设计中的表示重复，区域配额控制候选访问机会；二者本身均不保证时延下降或任务质量不变。

区域注意力需求促使我们将候选分配与评分表示分别考察。因此，本文关注区域页配额如何改变固定最终词元预算下的检索、共享紧凑坐标能否保留有用候选，以及注意力节省能否覆盖准备和选择成本。存档坐标诊断为这种区分提供动机，但不能将频率效应与坐标配对结构分离，也不能代表实际区域评分器的表现。逐层预填充统计同样为测试可选门控提供动机；门控属于近似策略，不假定预填充统计能够约束解码阶段的远区需求（补充注S6）。受ClusterKV词元／页视角~\cite{clusterkv}启发，图\ref{fig:pending-observation}展示Qwen3-8B归档稠密参考的距离密度与可行整箱捕获诊断。所观察的区域注意力保留率不同，但不能证明选择器保真或任务质量，现有得分与局部计时也不能隔离阶段效应或建立联合质量--时延优势。

Reported configuration-score differences do not isolate stage effects, and the separate synthetic timing study reports no latency advantage for shared-subspace scoring.
